content.content:
# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
  new hack for both.
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
  to reach them.
- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
  drift from the firmware's rule.
- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
  the clears that ran, for the tests.
- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
- Overlapping the push with the next frame (core 0 pushing while core 1

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).

  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
  new hack for both.

  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.

  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:

  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.

  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.

  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.

  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own

  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).

  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.

  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.

  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).

# Display, canvas and runner gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- M5GFX reads a plain `uint32_t` colour as RGB888. `TFT_RED` and friends are
  RGB565 constants. The canvas holds pixels already byte-swapped into the
  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits
  needs it (the logo loader, `dump_main.c`, tests). A hue-sweeping palette
  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.
- A hack that takes colour bits out of pixel values itself (Substrate's alpha
  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and
  without a crash. `substrate_single.c` swaps at `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground` so the hack sees ordinary RGB565; its golden-frame test
  fails if either is missing. Searching for `XGetPixel` finds none of this:
  dump every hack before and after a pixel-format change and `cmp` the frames.
  Pyro differs by a few hundred pixels, because it sorts projectiles by pixel
  value and so draws overlaps in another order.
- The display only gets the rows a hack drew. Every canvas write must go
  through `canvas_clear`, `canvas_point`, `hspan` or `canvas_paste_rect`
  (which record a span per row), or call `canvas_mark_dirty`, or the screen
  keeps the old pixels. The overlay text in `main.cpp` is the one deliberate
  bypass: it is written straight into `px`, marked by hand, and restored with
  `canvas_paste_rect`, which marks it again so the next push erases it.
  `test_push_present` replays every hack into a shadow display to catch a
  missed mark. M5GFX keeps a framebuffer for this panel and `endWrite` flushes
  one bounding box around everything written in a `startWrite` batch, so rows
  far apart must not share a batch (two corner pixels cost 11.7 ms together,
  0.1 ms apart). `push_plan` groups rows with a cost model fitted to device
  probes; its calibration shapes must include scattered rows, since compact
  rectangles cannot tell the models apart. Hacks that redraw unchanged pixels
  (CloudLife, Pedal) dirty nearly every row and gain little.
- The panel is round, so only the canvas's disc is pushed (issue #77).
  `canvas_set_disc` (in `main.cpp`) records each row's visible span: centre
  (w/2, h/2), and a pixel counts if any part of it is inside the circle.
  `push_plan` clips every dirty span to it and drops rows left empty. A hack
  with `sync_to_refresh` (Unknown Pleasures) still pushes whole rows, because
  its TE offset was swept for that push (#68). `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` turns off the
  push clip only, for an A/B: GL hacks still clear and fill only the disc
  (`gl.md`). Call `canvas_set_disc` before any `glshim_open`, which keeps a
  pointer to the spans. On the board: CloudLife's full frame 28.0 to 24.8 ms
  (26.2 to 28.4 fps), HexTrail 30.6 to 27.3 ms, Pyro 1.60 to 1.43 ms.
- Do not split a push into more batches than `push_plan`'s greedy grouping
  makes. Each extra flush in one push cost about 0.85 ms on the board, not the
  model's 17 us: a full disc frame in 19 bands took 39.9 ms against 24.7 ms in
  the greedy grouping's three, and per-row `pushImage` calls in one batch cost
  no more than one whole-image call (28.0 against 27.8 ms). The last flush of a
  push seems to finish while the hack draws its next frame; earlier ones are
  waited for. The cost model was fitted to single-flush pushes and cannot see
  this, so a split it rates cheaper can be slower.
- Hacks run on the Arduino `loopTask`, now set to a 16 KB stack in `main.cpp`.
  A hack with big local arrays can still overflow it (Rorschach's 9.6 KB did
  at 8 KB): the device reboots on that hack's first frame, and host tests
  cannot see it. Check the serial log for "Stack canary".
- `M5.update()` samples the buttons only when it runs and keeps no edge, so a
  press during a long hack step vanishes. `main.cpp` runs a 5 ms polling task
  on core 0 into `button_latch`, which needs the pin to hold a level for 30 ms.
  Reading the pin level inside a GPIO interrupt did not work: the release
  bounced and was counted as a second press. Check `press_waited` in the log.
- The runner caps a hack's delay at 10 s, and the loop credits only the push
  (31 ms; it was 41-45 ms between the byte-order fix and #23) against it,
  because a hack's delay is its pause after drawing. Compare device numbers
  with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: Pyro fell from 30 to
  23 fps with no change to Pyro.
- `runner_start` paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before
  `init`, as `screenhack.c` paints the window, or black if it has none.
  Substrate is white; every other hack asks for black or nothing.
- Overlay modes cycle on a tap: nothing, name badge, QR code, fps, battery. The
  badge, the QR code and the info line share the stamp/unstamp path, and
  `kPatchMaxH` (140) must cover the text block plus its outline: the badge
  is two lines, and `stampText` drops any line that would not fit. The
  battery is polled every 30 s (`M5.Power.getBatteryLevel()`; negative means a
  failed read, so the last good level stays). The QR code is encoded once at
  boot with M5GFX's `lgfx_qrcode` (`buildQr`, lowest version that holds
  `QR_URL`) into a 328 px white square, the biggest square inside the round
  screen. Each frame only copies it over the canvas and back (it reuses
  `infoPatch`, so that buffer is sized for the QR), and 328 rows are pushed
  every frame while it shows. The badge stamps 48 outline copies per frame and
  adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`. Read `wait=` as well as fps: a hack with
  delay slack (Galaxy) hides it, one running flat out (Squiral) does not.
- `lgfx_qrcode.h` (M5GFX's QR encoder, included at the top of `main.cpp`)

  because a hack's delay is its pause after drawing. Compare device numbers
  with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: Pyro fell from 30 to
  23 fps with no change to Pyro.
- `runner_start` paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before
  `init`, as `screenhack.c` paints the window, or black if it has none.
  Substrate is white; every other hack asks for black or nothing.
- Overlay modes cycle on a tap: nothing, name badge, QR code, fps, battery. The
  badge, the QR code and the info line share the stamp/unstamp path, and
  `kPatchMaxH` (140) must cover the text block plus its outline: the badge
  is two lines, and `stampText` drops any line that would not fit. The
  battery is polled every 30 s (`M5.Power.getBatteryLevel()`; negative means a
  failed read, so the last good level stays). The QR code is encoded once at
  boot with M5GFX's `lgfx_qrcode` (`buildQr`, lowest version that holds
  `QR_URL`) into a 328 px white square, the biggest square inside the round
  screen. Each frame only copies it over the canvas and back (it reuses
  `infoPatch`, so that buffer is sized for the QR), and 328 rows are pushed
  every frame while it shows. The badge stamps 48 outline copies per frame and
  adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`. Read `wait=` as well as fps: a hack with
  delay slack (Galaxy) hides it, one running flat out (Squiral) does not.
- `lgfx_qrcode.h` (M5GFX's QR encoder, included at the top of `main.cpp`)
  defines `MODE_*`, `ECC_*` and `LOCK_VERSION`, which clash with other code, so
  `main.cpp` `#undef`s them straight after the include. Its init returns
  nonzero when the text is too long for a version; `buildQr` tries versions 1
  to 40 and, if none fits, leaves `qrPixels` null so the tap cycle skips QR.
- Overlay text (`main.cpp`) is stamped into the canvas, pushed, then the
  pixels under it are restored. Drawing on the display after `pushImage`
  flickered badly, because the next push erases it. The canvas must end each
  frame exactly as the hack left it.
- Tearing. The panel scans its memory 60 times a second and `pushImage` is not
  synchronised with it, so for a refresh the top of the screen shows one
  picture and the rest another. A thin line that moves a few pixels a frame can
  fall in the gap and vanish for a frame (Unknown Pleasures' flicker: a flat
  stretch of one line gone for about 17 ms). The panel's TE line is on GPIO 38
  (`OLED_TE`), M5GFX programs it (`0x35`, `0x44` at line 466) and nothing waits
  for it. It pulses every 16.82 ms for 1.1 ms. A full push is 20.6 ms copying
  into M5GFX's framebuffer plus 11.7 ms flushing to the panel (split by an
  outer `startWrite()` around the `pushImage`; the flush happens at the
  `endWrite`). `HackEntry::sync_to_refresh` (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`) starts
  the push `kTeSyncOffsetUs` after TE rises (`runner/te_sync.h`). Only
  Unknown Pleasures asks, because it costs up to a refresh of latency a frame.
- The offset (7.4 ms) is the middle of the clean window, found by a sweep:
  eight offsets across one refresh, 3 s each, the step number stamped on the
  screen, filmed at 120 fps. 3.2 to 9.5 ms had no vanished line in 39 updates;
  1.1 and 15.8 ms did, with the seam at film row 495 and film row 268: about 107
  film rows per millisecond (the camera frame is taller than the panel; the
  466-row panel scans about 28 rows per millisecond), so the bad window is only
  about 5 ms wide. It is valid for a full-frame push (the 20.6 ms copy). A push
  of another size moves the flush and the sweep would have to be repeated: the
  QR overlay's 328-row push is one, so a seam may show while the code is up.
  `-DTE_DIAG` logs the TE period and where pushes start.
- `te_sync.c` trusts few edges. Once it knows the period it accepts a rising
  edge only within period/16 of a whole number of periods since the last, so a
  missed edge or a stray pulse cannot move the lock; four misfits in a row drop
  the lock and relearn it. An edge further ahead than one period is stale (the
  32-bit microsecond counter can pass half its range with the line dead), and
  waiting stops 100 ms after the last edge. The ISR is placed in IRAM, but
  Arduino's pin dispatcher and `gpio_get_level` are in flash; that is safe only
  because `CONFIG_ARDUINO_ISR_IRAM` is unset. The run log's `sync=` is the wait
  for the edge and is left out of `push=`: compare `push=` across hacks, and add
  `sync=` to get the frame's latency.
- Reading a film of the display: iPhone slo-mo files store their first and
  last seconds at normal speed, so the label changes every ~100 frames there
  and every 360 in the 120 fps middle. Stabilise against the scenery (four
  corner patches; a mask edge around the display pins phase correlation at
  zero), level the rows, and count a vanish only when a line is missing across
  at least three 24 px windows on one row and not in a settled frame of the
  same update. A detector that finds nothing must also find the event you know
  is there: mine reported zero until a known vanish was used as a control, and
  reported many false events on steep line stretches until settled frames were.
- Every push also dims the screen: the dimmest band falls to 0.86 of its
  settled brightness for about 25 ms (three camera frames at 120 fps), at 5 Hz,
  with or without TE sync (0.860 synced, 0.870 unsynced). It is probably the
  "whole screen redraws" flicker. Its cause is not known. Rod sees no dimming
  with the sparser build (20 rows of 50 points, a step of about 91 ms against
  165), so it may track how much is lit or how long the copy runs; not yet
  filmed (issue #68).
- A hack's returned delay is waited after the push, and only the push counts
  against it, so its own step adds to the frame time: to hold a rate, return
  the target minus the step (`ad_flyingtoasters.c`: 19.5 fps became 28.9).
- PSRAM cost model (`diag/psram_bench.h`, `-DPSRAM_BENCH`): the data cache is
  32 KB, 8-way, 32-byte lines over 80 MHz octal PSRAM, and every miss costs
  about 0.92 us whatever the write size (sequential about 35 MB/s). Firmware
  switches to 64-byte lines (4-way) when a hack starts (`dcache.h`, through
  ROM calls the SDK header says an application should not make): sequential
  passes get about 28% faster and the full-frame push drops from 29 to
  24.8 ms, but a lone short write costs 1.3 us a miss. Pinned A/B, two
  rounds each: Deluxe, Interference, Kumppa, Abstractile +9%, HexTrail +17%,
  Marbling +7%, WhirlWindWarp +6%, Qix and Hexadrop +4%, Gears +3%; Lisa,
  Substrate, XRaySwarm, Pyro, RotZoomer flat. A `sync_to_refresh` hack
  keeps 32 bytes (Unknown Pleasures' offset was swept against the old copy
  time) and so does a hack with `dcache_line32` set in its `HackEntry`
  (Discrete: -5% fps, step 67.9 to 72.8 ms, many short spans). The other core
  is parked in IRAM with interrupts off while the cache is reconfigured
  (`dcache_with_other_core_parked`, over `esp_ipc_call`), as the SDK does for
  flash writes: `noInterrupts()` stops only the calling core.
  `-DDCACHE_LINE32` turns it off for every hack. Compare builds only
  pinned: a free-running lap changes random parameters per visit and showed
  false regressions of 3x on five hacks. A ROM prefetch setting (trigger 1,
  size 0) changed nothing; other settings are untried.
- A hack with `repaints_all` (`hack_entry.h`) draws its next frame while core 0
  pushes the last (`runner/push_overlap.[ch]`, issue #54): two canvases swap
  each frame, the worker pushes the finished one, and the loop credits that
  push's measured duration against the hack's delay. Pinned A/B on the board,
  plain to overlapped: Deluxe 14.0 to 19.0 fps, Compass 18.8 to 29.1, FuzzyFlakes
  18.4 to 28.9, Moire2 16.5 to 26.4, Scooter 22.1 to 28.4; thirteen hacks are
  flagged (grep `repaints_all`, and `XLOCKMORE_HACK_REPAINTS_ALL`). The step
  slows by about 5 ms (both cores share the PSRAM cache), so the frame is
  roughly the step, not the longer of the two. Rules:
  - Flag a hack only if it never reads the canvas it starts from. The noise
    test and the real-swap test in `test_push_overlap` run every flagged hack
    for 300 frames; 40 frames missed Halo, which the 300-frame run caught. GL
    hacks fail them (TinyGL keeps `canvas->px`), as does GraphStat's swap run.
  - Only a gain of 5% or more on a pinned A/B earns the flag. Deco and CCurve
    are paced by their own delays and gained 0 and 2.6%.
  - A hack whose `HackEntry` comes from `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` in the
    byte-identical copy (Truchet, +25%) needs a wrapper to be flagged.
  - Any overlay (name, badge, QR, fps, battery) makes the push synchronous
    while it shows, so the fps overlay reads the plain rate. Read `fps=` in
    the serial log for the overlapped one.
  - Three bugs the spike hit: a redraw from the wait loop must not dispatch a
    second push (it blocked 25 ms), the overlay text canvas wraps one buffer
    and must follow `canvas.px`, and the newest-frame pointer must be dropped
    when a hack starts or Forest's first frame swapped the old picture back.
  - `-DPUSH_NO_OVERLAP` turns it off for every hack (the A side of `ab_flash`).
    The spare canvas is 434 KB of PSRAM; if it will not allocate the firmware
    pushes synchronously.

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- A `failed_ports.txt` name is the scorer's: the source file's stem
  (`companion` for Companion Cube), as the assessment's rows spell it. Check
  the cross appears after regenerating.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` stops with "hypnowheel: does not compile ... 'rotator.h'
  file not found": a dropped GL port counts in the backtest and is probed
  standalone, without the GL helpers' include path. `docs/speed-backtest.md`
  was last regenerated before Hypnowheel was ported, and was not regenerated
  for the CWaves batch either. The scorer also lists calls inside code that is
  never compiled (`XCreateBitmapFromData` in Cynosure's `DO_STIPPLE` block) as
  gaps.
- `score_hacks.py` skips the names in `OWN_HACKS` (our own hacks with no
  xscreensaver source, now `ad_flyingtoasters`) and still reports any other
  registry name it cannot scan as a typo. `speed_backtest.py` runs on the host
  only the registered hacks that have a device-measured row, so a `dump` build
  without the After Dark disk (which lacks the toasters) still works.
- `probe_hacks.MEASURED_ROW` takes only a number range in the fps cell: a
  row like `| HexTrail | 10.8-50.6, mean 15.3 |` is skipped, so the assessment
  shows `-` for its step and the backtest leaves it out. Put the mean in the
  prose.
- A call to an undeclared shim function also shows up as a gap named
  `error: incompatible integer to pointer conversion ...` (the implicit `int`
  return). It is noise beside the real gap (Barcode's `utf8_to_latin1`), but it
  counts towards the band.

# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): the random level generator recursed to ~315 KB
  and boot-looped the board, so a generated level is a copy from
  `hacks/pacman_pool.h` (24 levels, made on the host by
  `tools/pacman_levels.py` with the cells outside the round display walled
  off; the fixed level is still half of them), and the ghosts' route search is
  a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Re-run the tool after changing its mask or
  the generator's tile data. Each patch checks what it replaces. The two host
  pins that follow the game (`kBaseline`'s Pacman and the ghost-route chain)
  depend on how many `random()` values the level pick takes: re-take the chain
  with `pacman_loop_ai.c` temporarily including `pacman/pacman_ai.c`, then
  restore it and check the loop gives the same value. Its sprite sheet is
  built from `vendor/` into the build dir by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and
  never committed (3 MB as C text).
- Braid runs at 3-9 fps (0.8-2 before four rounds of work): it redraws every
  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.
- A hack can be freed before its first draw: two quick presses, or a press
  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`
  runs every hack through it. Blaster's free dereferenced NULL (it sizes a loop
  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a
  free that zeroes `NUM_ROBOTS` when `robots` is NULL.
- Deluxe is built through `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`, which includes the unmodified
  hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with overrides:
  `*transparent: False` (upstream's plane masks need colour planes, which
  `allocate_alpha_colors` reports none of) and `*doubleBuffer: False` (it was
  added when the shim drew only on the canvas, so the `XCopyArea` from its
  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).
  The wrapper then gives each throbber's GC an alpha of 26
  of 32 (upstream's translucent weight) and sends full wide circles to
  `stroke_circle`. A plain screenhack's `HackEntry` has no overrides unless a
  wrapper builds it. Its step is 45-63 ms on the device against a 32.5 ms push,
  so about 11-13 fps (14 with 64-byte cache lines); overlapping the push with
  the next step (`repaints_all`) takes it to 19 fps. Other ideas are in issue
  #54.
- Eight of the S-hack batch (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes,
  Halftone, Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole) are built through
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c` (pixmap double buffering, see `techniques.md`;
  LMorph's is `lmorph_single.c` because it needs no `HAVE_JWXYZ`). All but
  Anemotaxis and Wormhole, and Euler2D (`euler2d_single.c`), also use
  `single_precision.h` plus build-time float literals (`patch_float_literals.py`
  lists them). `single_precision.h` leaves `floor` and `ceil` on the double
  versions: Euler2D's wrapper maps them itself. After the literal pass the
  objects still showed soft-double helpers: Interaggregate's were `frand` in
  `build_field` (fixed with `single_frand.h`); Halftone's, Anemone's and
  Euler2D's are in `*_init` only, once a start. `tools/softdouble_report.py`
  lists them by function.
- To see which hacks are worth a look, flash a build with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=20`,
  log the serial port for one lap (about 40 minutes), and run
  `uv run tools/triage_hacks.py lap.log --soft` (after `pio run -e stopwatch`).
  It sorts each hack into step-bound, push-bound or paced (its own delay is the
  biggest part of the frame) and puts the soft-double calls in its object
  beside it. A hack that is step-bound with calls is a wrapper candidate;
  step-bound with none is in its drawing, not its maths (Braid, Marbling,
  Discrete, BinaryRing); paced ones gain only what the step saves, down to the
  delay (Forest 500 ms, Vines 200 ms). A wrapper that moves nothing is worth
  dropping: Bouboule built single stayed at 14.5 ms, because its cost is
  ellipse fills.

  differs, in registry order, so repinning several hacks takes one test run
  each (about 85 s), earliest first. A hack whose frames do not change under a
  wrapper (Compass and Halftone in single precision) keeps its hash.
- Anemone's step moved between 31 and 56 ms as its arms grew and shrank, so its
  fps was 11 to 15.5 whatever one 20 s window said. Upstream opens every frame
  by filling the whole window black, which is a full frame of PSRAM writes
  (229,000 pixels a frame on the host, the strokes only about 16,000 of them),
  so `anemone_direct.c` erases only where last frame's lines were

  same frames, and only those rows dirty. On the board, over one 20 s window
  per lap: 30.5 fps mean (worst 20.4), step 25.2 ms. Counting pixels and
  spans written a frame on the host (a temporary counter in `hspan`) is a
  quick way to see what a hack costs before the device does. Forest waits
  500 ms between trees by design (about 2 fps, and the push is 88 rows).

  before its 40 pixel margins, and xscreensaver reshapes it after): the wrapper

  fill that calls itself once for each blank cell, up to 360 deep in several
  puzzles, 32 bytes a level on top of the solver's frames. The build now
  replaces it with a loop over an explicit stack (frames identical to the
  recursive build). Read a puzzle hack's grid sizes, not just its frame size.

  upstream's 3,000 bees and 200 colours is up to 29 MB, which the host
  provided lazily and the board refused, so the hack drew one frame and
  nothing more. The registry gives it 120 bees and 8 colours. In single
  precision its flow dies out within about 600 frames (the screen stays
  black), so it is double: 3.0-4.8 fps, about 200 ms of every step being its
  search for the next flow. A single frame at 300 frames looked right in
  both: sweep several frame counts (300, 1000, 3000) for a hack that
  restarts itself or can die out.
- CCurve's `*limit` of 200,000 segments (each a malloc and a recursion) took
  740 ms in single precision and 2.9 s in double; the wrapper caps it at 30,000.
  Its 1.4 fps is its own pacing: 0.4 s between iterations, 42 ms of work.
- Droste (`droste_small.c`) hands back a loader token on the first call and
  finishes on the next, with the pixmap's size as the rectangle, so upstream's
  own "just finished" branch runs. It loads a picture the size of the window,
  not 2.5 times it (5.4 MB as the 32-bit image `XGetImage` makes), and renders
  at half width and height through `lowrez_put.h` (630 ms became 190 ms, 4.6
  fps). `XPutPixel` is mapped to swap the pixel, since `lowrez_put.h` wants
  ordinary RGB565 and the picture holds canvas order. MetaBalls takes all but
  28 KB of the internal heap while it runs (466 row buffers of 466 bytes).
- RotZoomer and Twang (`rotzoomer_single.c`, `twang_single.c`) start their
  picture and tiles the first time `draw` finds `load_image_async_simple`
  finished. The shim finishes at once and returns NULL, so that branch never
  ran and the first draw used a NULL zoom box (exit 139). Each wrapper does
  the finishing step straight after init. Changing the shim to return a loader
  would also change Boxfit and DecayScreen, so it is Rod's call. Both are
  single precision (they call `sin` and `cos` in double for every pixel).
  RotZoomer is unpinned in `test_hacks.c`: with no grab image every frame is
  black.
- BinaryHorizon (`binaryhorizon_swapped.c`) is told the display is 24 bits
  deep. Its 16-bit path adds less than a step of a channel per hit and rounds
  its random colour walk down, so every colour drifted to black or a dim
  green (as in BinaryRing). Pixels go straight to the window, and its image
  and pixmap are one pixel big, because nothing reads them. Every 30 s it
  restarts and callocs a new pixel buffer without freeing the old one (868 KB
  on the device): the wrapper frees it and clears the window.
- Munch defaults to `*xor: True`, so `XDrawPoint` honours `GXxor` now (only
  that primitive: lines and fills still copy). `pow2.h` is our own
  `i_log2` and `to_pow2`. IMSMap needed 1-bit `XYBitmap` images, `BitmapPad`
  is 32, and Deco needed `allocate_writable_colors` and `XStoreColors` (no
  writable cells). The scorer's gap lists were wrong twice: MetaBalls'
  `XListPixmapFormats` is under `#if 0`, and Ant needed only `automata.h`, a
  file in `hacks/` that is now copied to `xs_support/`.
- NerveRot passes the address of its own `double` locals to `rgb_to_hsv`, so
  its single-precision wrapper has an adapter (as Moire's). The restart test
  under AddressSanitizer found it as a stack-buffer-overflow, but a host frame
  looked right.
- Bouboule's upstream default is a red and a blue starfield for 3D glasses,
  drawn with `GXor`, which the shim does not do. The registry overrides
  `*use3d: False` (a single colour cycling through the palette) and
  `*cycles: 0`. Twang's 3 by 3 tiles of 120 pixels leave black margins and
  clip at the round bezel; `*tileSize` is the lever.
- A wrapper that finishes an image load itself (RotZoomer, Twang, Droste) must
  also handle the hack's timed reload, which the shim finishes at once too, so
  upstream's "just finished" branch never runs again. It must also match image
  layouts: `XGetImage` gives a 32-bit image, and a hack that memcpys it into
  its own 16-bit buffer shows alternating black pixels. RotZoomer did on the
  board until the trail review caught it. Test with a flat grab image and
  assert every pixel, then change the image before a timed restart.
- A wrapper that clears state before upstream's own timed check (BinaryHorizon
  frees its buffer) reads the clock separately from upstream, and the two reads
  can straddle a second. Read it once a frame and route upstream's `time()` to
  that reading with a function-like `#define time(p)`; test it with a fake
  clock whose second read is later.
- A hack that leaks on every in-hack restart (Munch's `get_string_resource`
  result) needs a restart-loop leak test of its own: `test_hacks` restarts only
  through start and stop.
- Deluxe's `draw_star` (ten sin/cos in software `double`, #54 idea 5): a
  single-precision build gave identical frames and no device gain (step
  45.06 vs 45.12 ms, pinned, 2 rounds). Skip it; the step is the blend, the
  mask and the strokes.
- Bubble3D is four files (`b_lockglue.c` holds `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, so the
  scorer knows it as `b_lockglue`; `SOURCE_STEMS` in `score_hacks.py` maps the
  registry name `bubble3d` to it), each built as its own `USE_GL` unit by
  `bubble3d_*gl.c`. Only `bubble3d.c` has a licence text; Rod chose to list the
  other four under its notice. The glue's `init()` builds a sphere and drops it
  (leaked on every start: the wrapper makes that call return NULL). A GL
  profile put 220 of a 300-390 ms step in a software-double `cos` per nudge
  axis per vertex: `bubble3d_bubble_gl.c` is single precision (frames
  byte-identical). Upstream's own `GLB_SLOW_GL` (set in `bubble3d_gl.c`) takes
  the sphere from 1,280 to 320 triangles: 4-5 fps became mean 11.5, worst
  window 8.2, with the push (12-24 ms, a full frame) now a fifth of the frame.
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_REPAINTS_ALL` fails both `test_push_overlap` checks, because
  TinyGL keeps drawing into the original `canvas->px` (issue #118). Upstream's
  default `transparent` skips the depth test and expects a blend TinyGL's fill
  does not do, so back faces overwrote front faces as a dark wedge in each
  bubble (found by the trail review): the registry overrides `*transparent:
  False`, which enables the depth test. It cost nothing measurable on the
  board (mean 11.5 before, 11.4 after).
